title: Mary close: do whatever he tells you
hook: every Marian title points back to her son

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Dormition: an icon of a son carrying his mother home. Your line was fell asleep. Who did you remember with that gentler word? Day one thousand three hundred fifty-six.

A wedding in Cana, a village in Galilee, and the party is going well, until the wine runs out. For the bride and groom, this is a disaster in front of everyone they know. The guests haven't noticed yet. The steward hasn't noticed. One guest has. Mary goes to her son and says, in the Douay-Rheims: "They have no wine." He answers her with something that sounds like a gentle refusal. And she doesn't argue. She turns to the servants instead, and what she tells them closes these days on Mary.
screen: `A WEDDING IN CANA.` → `THE WINE RUNS OUT.` → `THEY HAVE NO WINE.`

segments.voice: First, she notices. Nobody asked Mary to watch the wine. She sees a need in somebody else's house and carries it straight to her son. That's the picture Catholics have when they ask her to pray for them: someone who notices what's running out, and takes it to him. Second, she steps aside. Her words to the servants, in the Douay-Rheims: "Whatsoever he shall say to you, do ye." Not do what I say. Do what he says. Then she's out of the story. The servants fill the stone jars with water, carry some to the steward, and it's wine, the good wine, saved for last. Some readers notice that John's Gospel gives her no more lines after this. If so, her last words in it are an instruction to listen to someone else. Third, every title. Look back over these days. Mother of God, because of who her son is. Ever virgin, a life kept for him. Conceived without sin, by his grace. The new Eve beside the new Adam. Queen, because he is king. Taken up, because he rose first. The tilma, where she carries him. Lourdes and Fatima, where the message is pray. The Catechism puts it in one line: what Catholics believe about Mary rests on what they believe about Christ. Every name points past her. Fourth, what comes next. Tomorrow the path turns east, to the churches that pray in Greek, Arabic, Syriac and Slavonic and still stand with Rome. Mary goes with us there too, under the name the East gives her: Theotokos, the one who bore God.
screen: `SHE NOTICES WHAT'S RUNNING OUT.` · `DO WHAT HE SAYS, NOT WHAT I SAY.` · `EVERY TITLE POINTS PAST HER.` · `NEXT, THE CHURCHES OF THE EAST.` · then, large: `WHATSOEVER HE SHALL SAY TO YOU, DO YE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: do one thing he asks. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one thing Jesus asks in the Gospels that you already know: forgive. Love your neighbor. Give to the one who asks. Don't be anxious about tomorrow. Choose just one. Then let it get small and concrete: one person, one action, today. Hold that for a few breaths. If you pray, you can bring it to Mary the way the wedding did, and hear her line again: whatsoever he shall say to you, do ye. If you don't, simply hold the one thing, and decide when you'll do it. The bell holds the time.
Mary close. The end of the days on Mary, at a wedding in Cana, where the mother sends everyone to her son. Today's word.
Your line: she points to him. Today, do the one thing you chose in the practice, and do it before the day runs out. Day one thousand three hundred fifty-six.

howItsDone: Catholics read the wedding at Cana in the Mass and pray it as a Luminous Mystery of the rosary, and Catholic writers quote Mary's words to the servants when they explain devotion to her.

trapdoor: what you thought: a run of days that were all about Mary.
what it means: days of titles and places that each point past her, to her son.
what a scholar hears: John 2:5, her words at Cana, and the Catechism's principle that Marian teaching rests on what the Church believes about Christ (CCC 487).

sources.quoted: Whatsoever he shall say to you, do ye.

notes: Block E (days 1327–1356) is referred to as 'these days' with no count.

The look-back names titles taught across the block (Mother of God, ever virgin, Immaculate Conception, new Eve, queen, Assumption, the tilma, Lourdes and Fatima). Confirm each is described consistent with those days' scripts.
'Some readers notice that John's Gospel gives her no more lines after this': at the cross (John 19:25–27) Mary does not speak. Confirm.

Jesus's reply at Cana (John 2:4) is described as 'something that sounds like a gentle refusal' rather than quoted; readings of 'Woman, what is that to me and to thee?' differ. Confirm the description.
The look-ahead names Greek, Arabic, Syriac and Slavonic as languages of Eastern Catholic worship; confirm as a sample, not a list.
CCC 487 paraphrased: 'what Catholics believe about Mary rests on what they believe about Christ'. Confirm.
howItsDone: Cana is the second Luminous Mystery (added by John Paul II).
Editor pass: smoothed the hook's last lines ('the last thing we're going to hear her say in this whole block of days'), which read awkwardly aloud.
